title: Zika Virus Reprograms Microglial Mitochondrial Metabolism to Support Immune Activation and Viral Replication: Omega-3 DHA Counteracts Neuroinflammation and Viral Persistence

sections.abstract:
Microglial cells exhibit crucial metabolic adaptations to maintain neural homeostasis. However, their dysregulated activation during infections can lead to neurotoxicity and contribute to the development of neuroinflammatory disorders. Understanding the physiological and metabolic changes of microglia during immune activation is crucial for identifying protective targets against neuroinflammation. This study investigates how the Zika virus (ZIKV) alters microglia metabolism during inflammation, highlighting cellular adaptations that sustain oxidative metabolism linked to cell survival during cellular activation and viral replication. After identifying an enriched abundance of proteins related to oxidative phosphorylation and cellular component organization in the global proteomics of mouse brains following ZIKV exposure, we investigated the relevance of these pathways during in vitro infection of human microglia. ZIKV infection led to cytoskeleton remodeling via β-tubulin reallocation, which characterized an ameboid-like phenotype. Despite the indication of a shift toward increased glycolytic activity due to decreased intracellular glucose, which suggests its consumption, and the accumulation of tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) intermediates, ZIKV-infected microglia exhibit enhanced respiratory capacity and an abundance of smaller-sized mitochondria in the perinuclear region. The accumulation of citrate, succinate, and malate, while maintaining mitochondrial function, suggests an important metabolic adaptation that supports biosynthetic pathways and sustains cell viability under stress. Decreased intracellular glutamate abundance supports mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Pre-treatment with the anti-inflammatory docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) mitigates ZIKV-induced metabolic alterations by reducing pro-inflammatory markers, downregulating viral entry receptors, and lowering microglial activation and viral load. This study reveals that while ZIKV induces cell death in neuronal-like cells, the mitochondrial adaptation observed in microglial infection could be a key to maintaining cell survival throughout neuroinflammation. Our findings elucidate a novel cellular adaptation during ZIKV infection involving β-tubulin reorganization and metabolic dynamics, reflecting microglial flexibility and resistance during neuroinflammation, and demonstrating the therapeutic potential of DHA in mitigating ZIKV-induced pathology.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s12035-025-05418-y.

Keywords: Zika virus, Immunometabolism, Neuroinflammation, Metabolic adaptation, Mitochondrial dynamics
sections.introduction:
Microglia, the primary immune cells of the parenchymal Central Nervous System (CNS), exhibit remarkable metabolic adaptability [ 1 , 2 ]. Beyond their role in immunosurveillance, microglia contribute to critical processes, including angiogenesis, synaptic remodeling, axonal regeneration, and myelin repair [ 3 , 4 ]. However, under dysfunctional activation, microglia proliferate excessively and produce heightened inflammatory signals, leading to a neurotoxic profile commonly observed in various neuropathological conditions [ 5 ]. Microglial phenotypes shift dynamically during neuroinflammation characterized by distinct activation marker expression, cytokine and chemokine secretion, lipid droplet accumulation, and cytoskeleton remodeling associated with morphological changes [ 6 – 9 ]. These adaptations enable microglia to exist in diverse functional states [ 10 , 11 ]. Notably, microglia undergo significant metabolic shifts, adjusting their energy, lipid, and iron metabolism in response to inflammatory demands [ 12 , 13 ]. This metabolic flexibility, known as immunometabolism, allows microglia to dynamically regulate their bioenergetic needs to sustain their functional responses during inflammation [ 7 , 14 – 17 ]. As the first-line defense against invading pathogens in the brain, targeting microglial metabolic reprogramming throughout an infection could be the key to novel findings against neuroinflammation-induced damage.

The neurotropic virus Zika, classified as a flavivirus, is associated with the occurrence of the congenital Zika syndrome (CZS) and neurological complications in adults [ 18 – 20 ]. A key hallmark of ZIKV-related damage is neuroinflammation, driven by activation of glial cells, with microglia playing a pivotal role [ 21 – 23 ]. ZIKV has been identified as an inducer of the disease-associated microglial phenotype, characterized by molecular signatures related to pro-inflammatory processes observed in various neurodegenerative diseases [ 24 , 25 ]. Beyond inducing inflammatory markers, ZIKV is also recognized as a pathogen capable of reprogramming cellular metabolism. The virus was associated with an induction of mitochondrial dysfunction in neuronal-like cells [ 26 ], astrocytes [ 27 ], and placental cells [ 28 ], an effect that contributes to virus-induced cell death. However, despite the numerous reports on this phenomenon, there remains a gap in our understanding of metabolic disturbances that define the ZIKV infection in microglia. This knowledge could expand therapeutic possibilities for mitigating microglial-driven neuroinflammation, which has profound implications for maintaining neural homeostasis.

After detecting alterations in proteins associated with oxidative phosphorylation and cytoskeleton remodeling in the brains of ZIKV-infected mice, we investigated the role of these pathways in regulating the microglial response to ZIKV. In vitro infection of an adult human microglia cell line revealed ZIKV-induced β-tubulin accumulation around the nucleus, coinciding with an ameboid-like cellular morphology, further supporting the proteomic findings of enhanced cellular organization pathways following infection. Despite decreased intracellular glucose levels and the accumulation of tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) metabolites, which are usually found during the shift from oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to enhanced glycolytic activity, infected microglia exhibited increased respiratory capacity and a higher number of smaller mitochondria. Interestingly, we also observed decreased intracellular glutamate abundance, suggesting a mechanism of consumption that sustains mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Following the previously reported protective effects of polyunsaturated fatty acids against ZIKV pathogenesis, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) treatment effectively prevented virus-induced metabolic alterations and reduced viral load, alongside an induced decrease in the AXL receptor. This study highlights the striking physiological changes induced by ZIKV in microglia, influencing both protein expression and metabolite abundance throughout inflammation. The observed metabolic adaptations suggest a key role in sustaining microglial viability and proliferation, ultimately reinforcing prolonged pro-inflammatory signaling. Moreover, our findings provide evidence for the protective role of DHA in both preventing virus-induced metabolic dysregulation and reducing viral load, thereby promoting a less activated microglial profile.
sections.methods:
For ZIKV (PE243) (GenBank KX197192 ) virus expansion, Aedes albopictus C6/36 cells (ATCC CRL-1660) were cultured in TC-100 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and maintained at 28 °C without CO₂. The virus was initially propagated in C6/36 cells for a single passage before undergoing a subsequent propagation cycle in Vero cells (ATCC CCL-81), which were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 5% FBS. Viral stocks were aliquoted and stored at − 80 °C, with each vial used only once. Viral titers were determined by plaque-forming units (PFU) and confirmed by RT-PCR.

Wild-type (WT) C57BL/6 J male mice were housed in the Laboratory of Animal Breeding and Experimental Facility at the Institute of Biological Sciences, University of Brasília. The animals were maintained under a 12-h light–dark cycle at a controlled temperature (20–25 °C) with ad libitum access to food and water. Mice were intraperitoneally (i.p.) injected with Zika virus (ZIKV) at a viral load of 5 × 10 5 PFU/mL in a final volume of 500 µL. The control group (MOCK) received an equivalent volume (500 µL) of Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM). Each experimental group consisted of 5–6 animals. 14 days post-infection (dpi), mice were euthanized for further analyses. The experiments were conducted in accordance with Animal Protocol 12/2017, approved by University of Brasilia.

Each sample was subjected to a cell lysis process through heating (80 °C for 10 min) and sonication (5 cycles of 15 s at 60% power) in a buffer composed of 2% SDS, 0.1 mol/L DTT, and 0.02 mol/L TEAB. The protein extracts were then subjected to buffer exchange (with 8 mol/L urea, 0.02 mol/L TEAB at pH 8.5), reduction (0.1 mol/L DTT), alkylation (0.05 mol/L iodoacetamide), and digestion (1:100 trypsin in 0.02 mol/L TEAB, pH 7.9 for 9 h). The resulting peptides were desalinated using C-18 microcolumns and quantified using the Qubit system.

The obtained peptides were injected into a chromatographic system (Dionex Ultimate 3000 RSLCnano UPLC, Thermo, USA), configured with a trapping column (trap column) of 3 cm × 100 µm, containing C18 5 µm, 120 Å particles (ReproSil-Pur, Dr. Maich GmbH), connected in series to an analytical column of 24 cm × 75 µm, containing C18 3 µm, 120 Å particles (ReproSil-Pur, Dr. Maich GmbH). The samples were injected to obtain 1 µg on the column and subjected to a linear elution gradient between solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile), ranging from 2% B to 35% B over 155 min. The fractions separated in the chromatographic system were directly eluted into the ionization source of an Orbitrap Elite mass spectrometer (Thermo, USA), configured to operate in DDA (data-dependent acquisition) mode. MS1 spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap analyzer, with a resolution of 120,000 and an m/z range of 300 to 1650. The 20 most intense ions, above an intensity threshold of 3000, were fragmented, generating MS2 spectra in the ion trap analyzer via collision-induced dissociation (CID). Reanalysis of already fragmented ions was prevented through dynamic exclusion, enhancing the identification of less abundant peptides.

The obtained spectra were analyzed qualitatively and quantitatively to identify the total set of detectable proteins in the samples and to quantitatively evaluate the proteins that exhibited significantly different relative abundance between conditions. These proteins were further analyzed in greater detail to provide insights into the components that best distinguish between the conditions, and they were grouped according to pathways and interactions. All detected peptides are listed in Supplementary Material 1 . The spectra were analyzed using the Progenesis QI for Proteomics software (Waters, USA), where chromatogram alignment, peak area quantification (XIC—extracted ion chromatogram), normalization, and statistical analysis (ANOVA) of MS1 events were performed. Significantly different events ( p -value < 0.05) had their MS2 spectra submitted for identification using the Peaks software version 7.0 (BSI, USA). A database search was performed using the Uniprot repository data from May 2017, filtered for Mus musculus, tax. ID 10090, with redundant sequences removed using the FASTAtools software. The search was conducted based on de novo sequencing and PSM (peptide spectrum match), with FDR < 1%, at least 1 unique peptide, a precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm, and fragment tolerance of 0.5 Da, allowing up to 2 missed cleavages, with carbamidomethylation of cysteine as a fixed modification and methionine oxidation as a variable modification. Additionally, the Unimod modification search module was activated based on fragmentation patterns, along with a search for point mutations. After protein inference, quantification was refined based on the average of the peptides assigned to each protein, and statistical analysis at the protein level was performed, considering proteins regulated with an ANOVA p -value < 0.05. These proteins were subjected to multivariate analysis using PCA (principal component analysis) and clustering based on relative abundance profiles. As an additional stringency criterion, only proteins identified with two or more peptides were considered, and the second stage of statistical analysis was performed using the MetaboAnalyst platform [ 89 ]. Protein interactions were analyzed using the String program [ 90 ], and molecular pathways were analyzed through Reactome and Panther [ 91 ]. For these steps, protein accessions were mapped to gene codes using the Uniprot and DB2DB mapping platforms in BioDBnet [ 92 ].

Human microglial cell line C20 was developed by the research team led by Dr. David Alvarez-Carbonell at Case Western University [ 93 ]. The cells were cultured in a 1:1 mixture of DMEM and F12 medium (both from Sigma-Aldrich), supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 U/mL penicillin–streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich). Cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂.

C20 cells were pre-treated with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, Cayman Chemical) at a concentration of 12.5 µM and incubated for 1 h. As a control, cells were incubated with DMEM (2% FBS) in the absence of DHA. C20 cells, pre-treated and non-treated, were infected with ZIKV PE243 (MOI 1) and incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . The ensuing incubation persisted for intervals of 24, 48, 72, or 96 h, in alignment with the intended analysis timeline. Crucially, a parallel set of uninfected cells, referred to as unstimulated cells (UNS), were integrated as an experimental control.

C20 cells were plated in 96-well plates ( n = 3) and pre-treated (or not) with DHA and infected (or not) with ZIKV. After 48 and 96 h of infection, cell viability dependent on mitochondrial activity was evaluated by 3-(4,5-dimethyl-thiazol-2-yl)−2,5-diphenyl-tetrazolium bromide (MTT Sigma-Aldrich) in a concentration of 10% (5 mg/mL PBS). The plates were incubated for 1 h and then analyzed by spectrophotometry at 570 nm. The metric employed to quantify cellular response was the percentage of survival, explicitly gauged as the ratio of mitochondrial activity (as represented by luminescence values) in infected cells relative to the uninfected control group.

C20 cells were plated in 96-well plates and pre-treated (or not) with DHA and infected (or not) with ZIKV. After 48 h of infection, lactate dehydrogenase release was determined by measuring lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity in the cell supernatants using a commercial cytotoxicity assay (CyQUANT LDH cytotoxicity Assay). The assay measures LDH released from damaged cells, which catalyzes the conversion of lactate to pyruvate, generating a colorimetric reaction. The intensity of the color at 490 nm is proportional to LDH activity, while 680 nm serves as a background correction. Cytotoxicity was determined by comparing LDH levels in treated and infected samples to those in untreated controls (spontaneous release) and fully lysed cells, treated with lysis buffer provided by the kit (maximum release).

C20 cells were plated in 24-well plates and pre-treated (or not) with DHA and infected (or not) with ZIKV. After 48 h, they were marked with carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE) (Thermo Fisher Scientific), in a concentration of 5 µM diluted in PBS for 15 min protected from light at room temperature. After staining, cells were washed twice with PBS, followed by incubation with DMEM and F12 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum for 5 min. Pre-treatment (or non-treatment) and infections (as control uninfected cells) were made thereafter, and cells were incubated, protected from light, for 96 h. Proliferative capacity was analyzed by flow cytometry, using a FACSVerse. This experiment was performed in triplicate, each being repeated at least three times independently.

The C20 cells were plated on glass coverslips in a 24-well plate and, after 48 h of infection, were fixed with 3.7% Formalin for 30 min at RT. After two washes with PBS, the cells were incubated with anti-human AXL antibody (Abcam) at a 1:250 dilution overnight at 4 °C. Following incubation, cells were washed with PBS and analyzed on a FACSCalibur flow cytometer and analysis with FlowJo Version 9. For intracellular staining, after the fixation step described above, cells were permeabilized for 5 min with 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100 diluted in 1X PBS, followed by two washes with PBS. After permeabilization, the cells were incubated with the primary anti-human β-tubulin antibody (Invitrogen) at a 1:1000 dilution, or with anti-human phospho-NF-κb p65 (Invitrogen) overnight at 4 °C. Following incubation, the cells were washed twice with PBS, labeled with the secondary anti-Mouse Alexa Fluor 488 antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific), or anti-Rabbit Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), respectively. The cells were incubated for 2 h at 4 °C. After two washes, the samples were analyzed using the Leica TCS SP5 confocal microscope.

C20 cells were plated in a 24-well plate, pre-treated with DHA (or not), and infected (or not) for 48 h. After incubation, the cells were transferred to Eppendorf tubes and stained with 4,4-difluoro-1,3,5,7,8-pentamethyl-4-bora-3′,4′-diaza-S-indacene (BODIPY 492/595) (Sigma-Aldrich) using a 1:3000 working solution in PBS (v/v) for 30 min at 4 °C, protected from light. Following staining, the cells were washed twice with PBS, resuspended in a final volume of 500 µL of PBS, and stored at 4 °C until acquisition on a FACSCalibur flow cytometer and analysis with FlowJo Version 9.

C20 cells were plated in a 24-well plate with a round coverslip in each well. After the pre-treatment (or not) with DHA and infection (or not) for 48 h, cells were washed once with PBS and fixed with paraformaldehyde (1%) for 30 min at room temperature (RT). Next, they were washed three times with PBS and incubated with Bodipy diluted in PBS at 1:300 ( v / v ) at RT, for 30 min, protected from light. After staining, cells were washed three times with PBS, and 300 µL of 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) solution at 1:5000 in PBS ( v / v ) was added for 5 min, followed by three washes with PBS. The samples were analyzed using a Leica TCS SP5 confocal fluorescence microscope, and the average number and size were assessed using the ImageJ software.

Upon completion of the derivatization process, 100 µL of the samples was transferred to microvolume glass inserts for gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS), conducted using the Agilent 7890–5975 quadrupole GC–MS system equipped with an HP5-MS 30 m column (Agilent). The samples (1 µL) were injected in split mode (10:1) at 230 °C, with a continuous flow of 0.6 mL min −1 , using helium as the carrier gas. The oven temperature started at 70 °C for 5 min, and then increased to 350 °C at 5 °C/min before cooling to 330 °C. The obtained chromatograms were used toestablish a selected ion monitoring (SIM) method for detecting metabolites, including malate, fumarate, succinate, citrate, glucose, glutamate, and myo-inositol. Alignment and analysis of the metabolites were performed using MetAlign software and the MetaboAnalyst platform, respectively. Peak identification was conducted using the NIST MSSEARCH software and the NIST spectral library, and peak intensities were corrected for variations using the internal standard ribitol employed in the experiment.

Upon completion of the derivatization process, 100 µL of the samples were transferred to microvolume glass inserts for gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS), conducted using the Agilent 7890–5975 quadrupole GC–MS system equipped with an HP5-MS 30 m column (Agilent). The samples were injected in pulses (10:1) at 230 °C, with a continuous flow of 0.6 mL min −1 , using helium as the carrier gas. The obtained chromatograms were used for establishing a selected ion monitoring (SIM) method for detecting organic acids, such as malate, fumarate, succinate, citrate, glucose, glutamine, and myo-inositol. Alignment and analysis of the metabolites were performed using MetAlign software [ 94 ] and the MetaboAnalyst platform, respectively. Peak identification was conducted using NIST MSSEARCH software and the NIST spectral library, and peak intensities were corrected for variations using the internal standard ribitol employed in the experiment.

After 48 or 96 h of infection, secretion of the cytokines IL-6, TNF-α, and TGF-β, the chemokine MCP-1, all performed using BD Immunoassay reagents, was analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) following the recommendations of the manufacturer (BD Biosciences) and analyzed by spectrophotometry at 450 nM. This experiment was performed with an n = 4, each being repeated at least three times independently.

To evaluate the mitochondrial oxygen consumption, C20 cells were plated in a 24-well plate, DHA pre-treated (or not) and infected with ZIKV, using as control uninfected cells. After 48 h of infection, approximately 10 6 cells were suspended in DMEM/F12. Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was measured using a high-resolution respirometer (OROBOROS Oxygraph-2 k) at 37 °C, continuous stirring at 750 rpm, and a final volume of 2 mL. For calibration of the equipment, in each experimental day, DMEM/F12, the same medium used for cell culture, was used. The basal OCR was calculated upon stabilization of oxygen flux and after cell addition. Different inhibitors and uncouplers were added to the chamber containing cells and oxygen consumption was measured after stabilization of the signal. The following substrates were used: Oligomycin 1.25 µM, from which ATP-linked OCR could be obtained in the final analysis; carbonyl cyanide-p-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone (CCCP) in pulses of 100 nM, in order to analyze maximum respiratory capacity; and respiration was inhibited by antimycin-A 2.5 µM. The ATP-linked OCR was presented as the difference between the OCR before (basal respiration) and after (proton leaking) the addition of oligomycin.

C20 cells were plated on a coverslip, in a 24-well plate, and after 48 h of infection and treatments, the mitochondria of living cells were marked by MitoTracker Red CMXRos (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 45 min. After staining, the cells were vigorously washed with PBS and then fixed for 15 min with formalin (3.7%). After fixation, the cells were washed again and had their nucleus marked with DAPI for 5 min, in a DAPI/PBS ratio of 1:5000. After washes, the samples were analyzed using the confocal microscope Leica TCS SP5. Fluorescence quantification was performed using ImageJ software. This experiment was performed in triplicate, each being repeated at least three times independently.

For ultrastructural analysis, 1 × 10 4 cells were plated in 6-well plates. After ZIKV infection for 48 h, cells were washed with PBS and fixed overnight at 4 °C in a solution containing 2% paraformaldehyde (v/v), 2% glutaraldehyde (v/v), and 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer, pH 7.2. Subsequently, cells were post-fixed for 30 min in 2% osmium tetroxide (w/v) and 0.8% potassium ferricyanide (10 mM CaCl₂ in 0.2 M sodium cacodylate buffer). Samples were washed in distilled water and stained with 0.5% uranyl acetate for 24 h at 4 °C. The material was dehydrated in a graded acetone series (50–100%) for 10 min each and embedded in Spurr resin. Ultrathin sections were contrasted with uranyl acetate/lead citrate and observed under a JEOL 100 C and JEOL 1011 TEM at 80 kV.

Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) were measured using CellROX Green (Sigma-Aldrich) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After 24 h, 48 h, and 96 h of pre-treatment and infection, C20 cells were incubated with 5 µM CellROX for 30 min, protected from light at 37 °C. The cells were washed three times with PBS and incubated at 4 °C; fluorescence intensity was measured in the flow cytometry (FACS Verse) in the FL2 channel. The ROS generation was expressed as mean fluorescence intensity.

Viral load in serum and brain tissue was assessed using quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR). Brain samples were collected and subjected to RNA extraction using TRIzol (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich), following the manufacturer’s instructions. To improve RNA purity for viral RNA isolation, the upper aqueous phase was further purified using the RNeasy kit (Qiagen). After RNA isolation and purification, RT-qPCR was performed to quantify viral load, as previously described [ 26 , 95 ]. The positive control for ZIKV detection consisted of brain-derived RNA samples from immunocompromised mice infected with 10 4 PFU/mL. These samples were provided by the Central Laboratory of the Federal District and used as reference controls in the analysis. Serum samples were processed directly using the RNeasy kit without prior TRIzol treatment. A published primer set from Lanciotti et al. (2007) was used to detect ZIKV RNA and was additionally described by Correa et al. [ 34 , 96 ].

To monitor viral load in vitro , RNA extraction from C20 cells, either treated or untreated and infected with ZIKV, was performed using the High Pure Viral Nucleic Acid Kit (Roche Diagnostics). Quantification was carried out with a one-step qRT-PCR reaction using the LightCycler Multiplex RNA Virus Master (Roche Diagnostics). RNA standards were included, and reactions were performed in a final volume of 20 µL, with a primer concentration of 0.5 µM and a probe concentration of 200 nM. The experiment was conducted in triplicate and independently repeated at least three times. Viral RNA levels were normalized to GAPDH, and relative quantification was determined using the ΔΔCT (delta-delta CT) method, comparing experimental conditions to controls. Results were expressed as fold change, reflecting increase or decrease in viral RNA levels relative to the experimental control.

We performed statistical analysis using GraphPad Prism v9.0.0. To compare conditions between UNS and the ZIKV-infected condition, we used the unpaired Student’s t -test. Statistical significance was considered when p ≤ 0.05. To evaluate the effects of DHA during ZIKV infection, a two-way ANOVA was performed to assess both main effects and potential interactions between factors.
sections.results:
Since microglia play a central role in both health and disease, understanding their potential involvement in ZIKV-induced changes is crucial. To explore this, we first performed a global proteomics analysis of the mouse brain to identify molecular alterations that might indicate the involvement of microglia responses. Studying ZIKV in immunocompetent animal models is challenging, as mice are not naturally susceptible to the virus [ 29 , 30 ]. However, C57BL/6 wild-type (WT) mice can still be affected, though less than immunocompromised models [ 31 – 34 ]. To explore ZIKV-driven molecular changes, we intraperitoneally challenged WT C57/BL6 mice with 5 × 10 5 PFU/mL of ZIKV (PE243) and analyzed the animals 14 dpi.

Viral load assessment confirmed the absence of ZIKV in both serum and brain (Fig. 1 A and B). Additionally, brain weight showed no abnormalities (Fig. 1 C). Principal component analysis (PCA) plot obtained from global proteomics demonstrated a differential group of proteins distinguishing control and ZIKV-exposed brain, despite the absence of detectable viral RNA (Fig. 1 D). Proteins contributing to this differential profile were identified (Supplementary Table 1 ) based on the variable’s importance in the PLS-DA (VIP) score, which reflects each variable’s contribution to the model’s discriminatory power (Fig. 1 E). In the ZIKV-exposed group, an interesting protein cluster was observed, characterized by elevated abundance of the Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 7A2 (Cox7a2), which is an important factor for OXPHOS [ 35 ], and the Excitatory Amino Acid transporter 1 (EAAT1) (Slc1a3), a high-affinity glutamate transporter [ 36 ]. Further analysis of differentially modulated proteins also revealed the upregulation of Ubiquinol-Cytochrome C reductase and the ATP Synthase Subunit F6 (Supplementary Fig. 1 a), suggesting ZIKV exposure may impact OXPHOS activity.

Systemic ZIKV exposure changes the proteomic profile of mice brains. ZIKV RNA detection in the A serum and B brain tissue of mice infected (14 dpi) or not with the virus. C Brain weight of ZIKV-exposed or uninfected mice. D PCA of brain proteomic data, demonstrating distinct protein profiles between ZIKV-exposed and uninfected groups. E VIP scores from PLS-DA analysis of brain proteomic data collected from ZIKV-exposed or uninfected mice, highlighting key proteins, including Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 7A2 and EAAT1. F Heatmap of brain proteomic data collected from ZIKV-exposed or uninfected mice displaying the expression patterns of proteins associated with cytoskeleton remodeling and cell migration. G Enrichment analysis identifying cellular component organization as the most significantly enriched biological process

Interestingly, the analysis also revealed a differential abundance of proteins associated with cytoskeleton remodeling and cell migration. In the ZIKV-exposed group, an enrichment of Keratin, type I cytoskeletal 42 (Krt42) and Thymosin-β4 (Tmsb4x) was observed, alongside the downregulation of the Microtubule-associated protein 1A (Map1a) (Fig. 1 F). In agreement, the enrichment analysis provided by the WebGestalt platform indicated that cellular component organization was the primary enriched biological process, highlighting the role of cytoskeleton dynamics in distinguishing between ZIKV-exposed and control conditions (Fig. 1 G). These findings suggest that even brief systemic exposure to ZIKV can induce cellular changes in the brain 14dpi, potentially modulating processes related to cytoskeleton remodelling and metabolism. The proteomics analysis was performed using the entire brain, making it challenging to determine the specific cell type driving the observed changes. Nonetheless, these pathways are often associated with cellular activation, particularly in microglia, highlighting the importance of further investigating whether ZIKV induces similar physiological alterations in microglial cells to validate these findings.

Reliable in vitro models are essential for studying microglial responses in CNS disorders, though immortalized cultures lack the full complexity of brain microglia. Recently, a novel human microglial cell line (C20) derived from adult brain was introduced, demonstrating its potential for microglial physiology research by expressing classical morphological and immunological markers in response to different stimuli [ 37 – 39 ]. Thus, to investigate how ZIKV alters microglial physiology and the potential involvement of metabolic disturbances and cytoskeleton remodeling in viral pathogenesis, we infected the C20 cell line with ZIKV (MOI of 1) for 48 h. Infected microglia exhibited increased cell viability with no signs of cellular damage, as indicated by unchanged lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release (Fig. 2 A and B). Additionally, ZIKV infection led to a decrease in CFSE fluorescence, indicating increased microglial proliferation, which persisted from 48 to 96 h post-exposure (Fig. 2 C and Supplementary Fig. 2 a). To verify how cell viability would be affected after a prolonged viral exposure, which is usually associated with a cytotoxic effect, the infection with MOI 1 was verified for both microglial cell lines and neuronal-like cells (SH-SY5Y) after 96 h of viral exposure (Supplemental Figure 2 b). Vero cells were included as a control for virus-induced cytopathic effects, as they are commonly used as a reference cell line in virology. The data showed that neuronal-like and Vero cells exhibited around a 50% decrease in cell viability, while microglial cells showed only a 20% decrease, suggesting greater resistance to virus-induced cytotoxicity. Additionally, 48 h after infection, AXL expression—a key receptor implicated in ZIKV entry into various brain cells [ 40 ]—was upregulated by 40%, potentially facilitating viral entry and further infection spread (Fig. 2 D).

ZIKV infection induces lipid droplet biogenesis, NF-κB translocation, and β-tubulin remodeling in microglial cells. A Cell viability evaluation (MTT assay) and B LDH release levels in ZIKV-infected (MOI1) and unstimulated (UNS) microglial cells (C20) after 48 h of infection. C CFSE flow cytometry analysis of cell proliferation of cells infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV. D AXL receptor expression in cells infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV analyzed by flow cytometry, represented by mean fluorescence intensity (MFI). E Lipid droplet (LD) biogenesis assessed by BODIPY 492/595 staining for flow cytometry (representative histogram) and spectrophotometric quantification via Oil Red O staining of cells infected or not with ZIKV. F Staining with BODIPY 492/595 (LD, green) and DAPI (nucleus) of cells infected or not with ZIKV for confocal microscopy analysis. G and H Average lipid droplet number and size estimated using ImageJ. I NF-κB translocation to the nucleus assessed by confocal microscopy (NF-κB in green, nucleus in DAPI) of cells infected (12 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV. J Staining with anti-β-tubulin (green) and DAPI (nucleus) of cells infected or not with ZIKV to analyze morphological changes in microglia

Lipid droplet (LD) accumulation is a well-established marker of microglia proinflammatory activation [ 16 , 41 ]. To assess LD biogenesis following ZIKV infection, Bodipy and Oil Red O staining were performed, which revealed a 1.3-fold increase in LD content compared to the control group (Fig. 2 E–H). Additionally, confocal microscopy confirmed a significant accumulation of LDs in ZIKV-infected cells, showing a tenfold increase in the average number of LDs per cell, while the average LD size remained unaffected. To further confirm microglial activation, nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) translocation from the cytoplasm to the nucleus was evaluated via confocal microscopy at 12 h post-infection (Fig. 2 I). In unstimulated cells, NF-κB staining was primarily cytoplasmic, whereas infected microglia showed elevated nuclear staining of NF-κB, indicating the translocation of this key transcription factor. Consistently, ZIKV-infected cells showed a significant increase in NF-κB-related inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and TNF-α, compared to control cells (Supplementary Fig. 4 a and b).

To determine whether ZIKV-induced microglial activation markers would involve cytoskeleton remodeling and subsequent morphological changes in microglial cells, β-tubulin staining was performed 48 h post-infection (Fig. 2 J and Supplementary Fig. 3 a). Infected cells exhibited a distinct morphology shift, with a reduced frequency of ramified cells compared to the control. Interestingly, a unique β-tubulin pattern was observed in ZIKV-infected cells, where the protein transitioned from an asymmetric distribution to a perinuclear accumulation. This was evident from the increased β-tubulin staining around the DAPI-stained nucleus in infected cells compared to controls. This finding highlights the role of β-tubulin rearrangement in microglial morphological changes during infection and further supports the previous proteomic analysis, which identified cytoskeleton remodeling as a key pathway enriched after ZIKV exposure (Fig. 1 D). The data also raised important questions about whether this cytoskeleton reorganization influences the localization of other organelles, particularly mitochondria, which play a central role in cellular dynamics during inflammation and infection. Given the significance of this phenomenon, we next investigated mitochondrial dynamics to gain important insights regarding its potential impact on microglial function.

To investigate how mitochondrial function is affected in ZIKV-infected microglia, the respiratory capacity was assessed 48 h post-ZIKV exposure (Fig. 3 A–D). The data reveal that basal, ATP-linked respiration and spare respiratory capacity remained unaffected. However, when maximal respiration was induced using CCCP, infected microglia exhibited a 1.5-fold increase in respiratory capacity compared to control cells. These findings suggest that, under normal conditions, mitochondrial bioenergetic parameters remain comparable between infected and uninfected microglia. However, under metabolic stress or increased energy demands, ZIKV-infected microglia exhibit enhanced oxygen consumption. This adaptation may help sustain cell viability and function during infection.

ZIKV infection induces mitochondrial and metabolic adaptations in microglial cells. A – D Microglial cells (C20) infected (48 h) or not with ZIKV in a MOI of 1 were investigated in terms of A oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and B ATP-linked respiration using a high-resolution respirometry assay in the presence of the inhibitors oligomycin (1.25 µM), CCCP (100 nM), and antimycin A (2.5 µM). E Staining of cells infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV using MitoTracker CMRox (red) and DAPI (nucleus) for confocal microscopy analysis of mitochondrial distribution. F Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) assessment of mitochondrial morphology of cells infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV. Enlarged mitochondria are indicated by Δ, and smaller-sized mitochondria by *. G ImageJ quantification of red fluorescence intensity indicative of mitochondrial content of cells infected or not with ZIKV. H – J Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in cells infected (48 h, 72 h, and 96 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV, assessed by live-cell staining with CellRox Green and flow cytometry analysis. K – L Metabolic profile analysis of cells infected or not with ZIKV (48 h post-infection) using GC–MS, represented by plots presenting metabolites’ relative abundance

To investigate the distribution of mitochondria in ZIKV-infected microglia, cells were stained with MitoTracker Red CMXRos and analyzed via confocal microscopy (Fig. 3 E). In control cells, mitochondria were widely distributed throughout the cell body. In contrast, infected cells showed an accumulation of mitochondria in the perinuclear region, which might be associated with the morphological changes described earlier (Fig. 2 J). Despite this differential localization, quantification of fluorescence intensity revealed higher mitochondrial staining in infected microglia compared to control cells, suggesting an increase in mitochondrial content following infection (Fig. 3 G). To further investigate these changes, microglial cells were analyzed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Fig. 3 F). The analysis confirmed a higher mitochondrial density in ZIKV-infected cells compared to control cells, as demonstrated by the higher frequency of these organelles in the cytoplasm (Fig. 3 F). Notably, mitochondrial morphology differed significantly between the groups: while control cells predominantly contained elongated mitochondria (indicated by ∆), infected cells exhibited a higher number of smaller mitochondria (indicated by *), suggesting a shift in mitochondrial dynamics, as further determined by the size distribution analysis (Supplementary Fig. 4 f and 4 g). In line with these findings, the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) was assessed by CellROX staining at distinct time points post-infection (Fig. 3 H–J). At early time points (24 to 48 h), ROS levels were reduced, despite the increased mitochondrial content and oxygen consumption. However, by 96 h post-infection, ROS production significantly increased, which may be attributed to cytoplasmic, rather than mitochondrial sources—a phenomenon commonly associated with prolonged cellular activation.

Given that mitochondrial function and morphology during ZIKV infection, the detection of metabolites associated with glucose metabolism was performed using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) to evaluate the metabolic consequences of these changes at 48 h post-infection. This time point was selected because early cellular disturbances typically precede the onset of cytotoxicity. For instance, mitochondrial dysfunction has been observed at early stages of ZIKV infection in neuronal-like cells, preceding apoptosis, which becomes evident around 96 h post-infection [ 26 ]. Given that microglial cells exhibited greater resistance to the virus, we hypothesized that assessing their metabolic state at an earlier time point could provide important insights into how these cells maintain viability and mitochondrial function during the infection.

Analysis revealed a significant increase in tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates, including succinate, malate, fumarate, and citrate, in infected cells compared to controls (Fig. 3 K–N). Importantly, the abundance of intracellular glucose was decreased after infection, suggesting higher consumption compared to control cells (Fig. 3 O). The increased glucose metabolism, followed by the accumulation of TCA cycle intermediates, is often observed during enhanced glycolytic activity, where cells reduce OXPHOS and increase the glycolysis rate even in the presence of oxygen [ 42 ]. However, high-resolution respirometry indicated that OXPHOS remained intact, despite the accumulation of TCA cycle intermediates. To identify potential alternative metabolites supporting OXPHOS and ATP production, the metabolic profile was assessed. Alanine and valine levels remained unchanged between infected and control cells, suggesting that their metabolism does not play a central role in microglial metabolic adaptation (Supplementary Fig. 4 c and d). In contrast, a slight decrease in glutamate abundance was observed, suggesting increased glutamate consumption, potentially supporting OXPHOS and mitochondrial function in infected cells (Fig. 3 P). These findings indicate that ZIKV infection changes microglia metabolism, promoting enhanced glucose utilization while sustaining OXPHOS and mitochondrial integrity through glutamate consumption.

To gain novel evidence that ZIKV-induced microglial alterations were primarily driven by inflammatory signaling in response to the infection, it was hypothesized that pre-treatment with an anti-inflammatory molecule could mitigate these effects. Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), a well-known anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA), is widely considered a promising molecule counteracting neuroinflammation [ 43 , 44 ]. DHA has been reported to protect against ZIKV infection in neuronal-like cells [ 26 ] and in vivo models [ 45 ], in addition to its broad anti-inflammatory effects on microglial cells, abrogating inflammation. To test this, microglial cells were pre-treated with DHA (12.5 µM) for 1 h before infection, and mitochondrial viability was assessed 48 h post-infection. Results showed that DHA preserved mitochondrial viability, maintaining it at levels comparable to uninfected control cells during ZIKV infection (Fig. 4 A). Additionally, DHA significantly reduced the proliferative capacity of the infected cells compared to untreated infected cells, as indicated by the approximately 9% decrease in mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) (Fig. 4 B). Importantly, this reduction in proliferation was not associated with compromised cell membrane integrity, as LDH release remained unchanged (Fig. 4 C). The consistent LDH levels confirm that neither ZIKV infection nor DHA treatment caused cytotoxicity, reinforcing the idea that the observed decrease in proliferation resulted from DHA’s regulatory effects rather than cellular damage.

DHA treatment protects against ZIKV-induced microglial proliferation and cytoskeleton remodeling. A Mitochondrial viability of microglial cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not with ZIKV (48 h post-infection) in a MOI of 1). B Proliferative capacity of cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not with ZIKV (48 h post-infection) evaluated by CFSE staining and flow cytometry. C Cell membrane integrity assessed by LDH release of cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not with ZIKV (48 h post-infection). D – F Staining with BODIPY 492/595 (LD, green) and DAPI (nucleus) of cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not with ZIKV for confocal microscopy analysis. G Staining of cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not with ZIKV (48 h post-infection) with anti-β-tubulin staining (green) and DAPI (blue—nuclei for confocal microscopy analysis)

To further assess microglial activation, LD biogenesis was evaluated using confocal microscopy, quantifying both LD number and size (Fig. 4 D–F). The analysis revealed that DHA pre-treatment reduced by approximately 40% compared to infected cells without intervention. Additionally, β-tubulin organization was assessed via confocal microscopy at 48 h post-infection. The results demonstrated that DHA pre-treatment prevented β-tubulin reorganization within the perinuclear region, effectively attenuating cytoskeleton remodeling and preserving cellular morphology similar to that of control cells (Fig. 4 G). These findings indicate that DHA can mitigate ZIKV-induced microglial activation, particularly by reducing LD accumulation and cytoskeletal alterations. However, to confirm whether DHA effectively suppresses ZIKV-induced inflammation, further analysis of specific inflammatory markers is necessary. This will determine the extent to which DHA’s anti-inflammatory properties reduce microglial inflammation during viral infection and contribute to maintaining cellular homeostasis.

After establishing that DHA pre-treatment prevents ZIKV-induced physiological changes in microglia, we next evaluated whether it also modulates cytokine release, thereby reducing soluble inflammatory markers. Our results showed that DHA significantly attenuated the production of the key pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6, and the chemokine MCP-1, during ZIKV infection. Additionally, there was a slight increase in the anti-inflammatory cytokine TGF-β (Fig. 5 A–C). These findings demonstrate that DHA mitigates ZIKV-induced inflammation by downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoting an anti-inflammatory response, suggesting a regulatory role in microglial activity during infection.

DHA attenuates inflammatory markers in microglial cells during ZIKV infection. A – D Quantification of the secretion of pro-inflammatory (IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (TGF-β) by microglial cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not (48 h post-infection) with ZIKV via (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) ELISA

To determine whether DHA pre-treatment influences microglial metabolism during ZIKV infection, the abundance of key intermediates from the TCA cycle was assessed by GC–MS. Notably, DHA alone did not significantly alter the levels of succinate, malate, fumarate, or citrate compared to control cells (Fig. 6 A–D). However, DHA pre-treatment before ZIKV infection effectively prevented the virus-induced accumulation of malate and fumarate, maintaining their levels comparable to those of control cells. A similar protective effect was observed for intracellular glucose and glutamate, where DHA pre-treatment counteracted the ZIKV-driven reduction in their abundances (Fig. 6 E and F). Interestingly, intracellular lactate levels were elevated in DHA-treated infected cells, suggesting a metabolic adaptation induced by DHA (Fig. 6 G). Additionally, PUFAs from the n-3 and n-6 classes share common enzymatic pathways involved in the synthesis of their respective derivatives [ 46 , 47 ]. Since DHA belongs to the n-3 PUFAs class, its increased availability is often associated with a reduction in n-6-derived metabolites due to enzymatic competition. As expected, arachidonic acid (ARA) (Fig. 6 H), a derivative of the n-6 series, was specifically reduced in DHA-treated infected cells.

DHA protects against ZIKV-related changes in microglial metabolism during infection. TCA cycle intermediates (malate, fumarate, succinate, and citrate) ( A – D ), intracellular glucose and glutamate levels ( E – F ), intracellular lactate levels ( G ), and arachidonic acid (ARA) levels ( H ) were measured. I Staining of cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV using MitoTracker CMRox (red) and DAPI (nucleus) for confocal microscopy analysis of mitochondrial distribution. J – M Mitochondrial respiration of cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected or not with ZIKV was assessed using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros), via the measurement of basal, ATP-linked, spare, and maximal respiratory capacity. Enlarged mitochondria are indicated by Δ, and smaller-sized mitochondria by *

To investigate whether DHA’s protective effects against ZIKV-induced metabolic alterations extend to mitochondrial distribution, microglial cells were stained with MitoTracker Red CMXRos after 48 h of viral exposure (Fig. 6 I). Confocal microscopy revealed that DHA pre-treatment prevented the perinuclear accumulation of mitochondria observed in ZIKV-infected cells, instead maintaining widespread mitochondrial distribution throughout the cell body and microglial ramifications, similar to that of unstimulated cells. Mitochondrial function was further assessed using high-resolution respirometry to evaluate whether DHA mitigates ZIKV-induced alterations in respiratory parameters. As previously observed (Fig. 3 A and D), neither basal nor ATP-linked respiration was affected by ZIKV infection alone or by DHA treatment (Fig. 6 J and K). However, DHA preserved both spare respiratory capacity (Fig. 6 L) and maximal respiratory capacity (Fig. 6 L and M) at levels comparable to those of unstimulated cells, preventing the ZIKV-induced increase in mitochondrial stress response. Finally, mitochondrial morphology was examined via TEM to assess whether DHA could counteract the ZIKV-driven increase in smaller mitochondria, as earlier observed in Fig. 3 F. As expected, ZIKV-infected cells predominantly exhibited smaller mitochondria (Fig. 6 N). However, DHA-treated infected cells displayed an intermediate phenotype, characterized by a mix of smaller mitochondria and a higher frequency of enlarged mitochondria, which were distributed throughout the cell body rather than clustering in the perinuclear region. Interestingly, although DHA treatment alone did not lead to significant changes in cellular metabolism and other previously assessed parameters, TEM assessment revealed an increased number of smaller mitochondria. This suggests that DHA may influence mitochondrial dynamics even under homeostatic conditions. In the context of ZIKV infection, DHA effectively counteracts ZIKV-induced alterations in mitochondrial distribution, morphology, and bioenergetics, thereby preserving cellular homeostasis during infection.

Previous studies have reported that DHA reduces viral detection in neuronal-like cells [ 26 ], suggesting an antiviral role. Consistently, our data showed that DHA pre-treatment reduced ZIKV RNA levels by approximately 50%, indicating a significant decrease in viral load within microglial cells (Fig. 7 A). Interestingly, DHA also led to a 25% reduction in AXL expression on the cell membrane (Fig. 7 B), a key receptor implicated in ZIKV entry. This suggests that DHA may impair viral entry by downregulating AXL, thereby limiting infection. Transmission electron microscopy further confirmed these findings, revealing organized viral particles in ZIKV-infected microglia, as typically observed during viral infections. However, in DHA-treated cells, fewer viral particles were detected after 96 h of infection, in agreement with the qPCR results. This suggests that DHA may interfere with ZIKV entry or replication, ultimately reducing viral burden. Overall, these findings indicate that DHA protects microglial cells from ZIKV-induced alterations by lowering viral load, thereby mitigating inflammatory responses and reducing the metabolic adaptations required to sustain cell viability and activation during infection.

B AXL receptor expression in cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV, assessed by flow cytometry. C Viral particle organization in cells pre-treated or not for 1 h with DHA (12.5 µM) and infected (48 h post-infection) or not with ZIKV, analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (scale bar, 0.2 µm)
sections.discussion:
This study provides experimental evidence that even a brief systemic exposure to ZIKV in an immunocompetent animal model can lead to an increased abundance of proteins related to OXPHOS and the enrichment of pathways associated with cellular organization in the brain. Given the well-established plasticity of microglia in response to inflammatory challenges, we hypothesized that microglia are the primary cells exhibiting this phenotype. In vitro infection of microglial cells revealed that ZIKV enhanced mitochondrial maximal respiratory capacity, promoting sustained cellular viability, proliferation, and viral replication even at later stages of infection. The observed decrease in glucose and glutamate levels, coupled with the accumulation of TCA cycle intermediates, highlights a notable metabolic adaptation typically associated with elevated glycolytic respiration. However, despite this metabolic shift, mitochondrial OXPHOS remained functional, suggesting that microglia adjust their metabolism to meet the energy demands of infection while maintaining bioenergetic efficiency. This adaptation allows microglial cells to remain functional and viable while simultaneously supporting viral replication, demonstrating their dual role in ZIKV pathogenesis, both exacerbating neuroinflammation and acting as a reservoir for viral particles.

Studying ZIKV infection in animal models presents a significant challenge, as immunocompetent models generally fail to sustain viremia, leading most studies to rely on immunocompromised models [ 30 ]. However, research has shown that pathogenesis can still occur in immunocompetent models, albeit with less pronounced effects, particularly in tissues such as the placenta and gut [ 34 , 48 , 49 ]. Consistent with these findings, our study demonstrates that intraperitoneal (IP) infection of C57BL/6 WT mice with ZIKV resulted in proteomic alterations in the brain, even in the absence of detectable viral load at 14 dpi. To understand how systemic exposure to ZIKV affects the brain, it is essential to consider how peripheral infections activate neural circuits, signaling the brain about emerging inflammatory responses. Recent studies have further characterized the body-brain neural axis, highlighting the role of vagal neurons in sensing both inflammatory and anti-inflammatory signals [ 50 , 51 ]. These responses can modulate neuronal populations and influence microglial polarization in the CNS. Notably, previous research has shown that ZIKV can directly target peripheral neurons in vivo , potentially explaining virus-related symptoms, such as abdominal pain mediated by sensory neurons [ 52 ]. Based on these findings, it was hypothesized that this body-brain axis may explain how ZIKV induces brain changes without direct virus presence in brain tissue. Microglia may play a central role in sensing and responding to peripheral and inflammatory signals, contributing to the observed proteomic alterations. Given their involvement in cellular rearrangements and mitochondrial metabolism, microglia were chosen for further characterization to investigate how ZIKV infection impacts these enriched pathways identified in our proteomic analysis.

In this study, we demonstrated that, unlike neurons and astrocytes [ 26 , 27 ], immortalized human microglia derived from adult brain maintain cellular viability throughout ZIKV infection, consistent with previous reports [ 53 ].

Infected microglia exhibited hallmarks of cellular activation, including increased proliferation, lipid droplet biogenesis, and NF-κB nuclear translocation, while maintaining cell viability at earlier time points, and preventing excessive loss at later stages, compared to neuronal-like cells. ZIKV exposure also induced significant morphological changes, with microglia transitioning from a ramified to an amoeboid shape, a characteristic of activated microglia [ 4 , 8 ]. Strikingly, β-tubulin staining revealed a pronounced accumulation of the protein near the nucleus in ZIKV-infected cells, whereas control cells displayed a more evenly distributed staining of the β-tubulin network. This phenotype aligns with previously reported microtubule cytoskeleton dynamics, which are recognized as hallmarks of reactive microglia following lipopolysaccharide and interferon-γ stimulation [ 11 ]. Cytoskeleton remodeling plays a crucial role in allowing macrophages and microglia to acquire the distinct morphologies [ 54 ], with the tubulin network contributing to microtubule assembly and disassembly. This process is regulated by microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), which were coincidentally found enriched in the brain of ZIKV-infected mice, as identified in our proteome analysis. These findings highlight the essential role of cytoskeleton components in enabling microglial morphological adaptation following ZIKV exposure, reinforcing the concept that cellular organization pathways are pivotal in microglial responses to infection.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are well-documented consequences of ZIKV infection in various cell types, including trophoblasts [ 55 ], neuronal-like cells [ 26 ], and astrocytes [ 27 ]. Given this, we initially expected ZIKV infection to impair mitochondrial function in microglia, particularly due to the cellular activation induced by the virus. In immune cells, activation is often accompanied by a metabolic shift from OXPHOS to glycolysis to rapidly meet increased energy demands and provide biosynthetic precursors essential for pro-inflammatory functions [ 7 , 17 , 23 , 56 – 58 ]. Importantly, at earlier time points, such as 48 h post-infection, ZIKV appeared to induce an increase in cell viability as measured by the MTT assay. This assay relies on the reduction of the tetrazolium salt to formazan by cellular dehydrogenases, particularly those associated with NADPH and glycolytic enzymes in metabolically active cells [ 59 – 61 ]. Therefore, in addition to assessing cell viability, the MTT assay also reflects how actively the cells are in generating NADH/NADPH through glycolysis-related pathways. As such, a higher MTT signal may indicate not only increased viability but also elevated glycolytic flux [ 59 ].

However, despite clear evidence of ZIKV-induced microglial activation, mitochondrial respirometry analysis revealed that mitochondrial function remained intact, even during late infection. Moreover, both maximal and spare respiratory capacity were significantly increased following infection. These findings suggest that rather than impairing mitochondrial function, ZIKV enhances mitochondrial oxygen consumption during microglial activation, sustaining OXPHOS. Curiously, a recent study has shown that rotenone-mediated inhibition of mitochondrial respiration in JEG-3 cells suppresses ZIKV replication, emphasizing the reliance of the virus on the maintenance of the electron transport chain to fulfill its requirements for replication [ 62 ]. To better interpret these results, it is important to consider that, beyond metabolic reprogramming associated with classical inflammatory activation, viral infections frequently hijack immune cell metabolism to support viral replication, as demonstrated for several pathogens [ 63 – 65 ]. This distinction is essential when analyzing microglial metabolic shifts, as viral presence itself can drive unique metabolic adaptations that differ from those seen in resting or classically activated microglia. For instance, chronic human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infection has been shown to increase mitochondrial biogenesis, even under conditions of enhanced glycolytic respiration [ 66 , 67 ]. Additionally, HCMV-infected cells exhibited elevated mitochondrial activity, primarily driven by increased glutamine conversion to α-ketoglutarate, which fuels the TCA cycle despite the predominance of glycolytic respiration [ 68 ]. This dual metabolic strategy supports both immune evasion and viral replication. Similarly, in this study, ZIKV-infected microglia displayed an accumulation of TCA cycle intermediates and a decrease in intracellular glucose, indicative of a broken TCA cycle and elevated glycolytic respiration [ 69 ]. However, since mitochondrial respiration remained functional, we hypothesized that the observed decrease in intracellular glutamate reflects its role as a fuel source for the TCA cycle, mirroring metabolic adaptations in other viral infections [ 70 ]. Additionally, accumulated citrate can fuel fatty acid synthesis [ 71 ], thus supplying lipid droplet biogenesis following infection. In turn, malate can contribute to the maintenance of the redox system [ 72 ], which may be involved in the control of oxidative stress observed in our model at early time points. These findings suggest that ZIKV employs a unique metabolic strategy in microglia, balancing immune activation and bioenergetic reprogramming that represent a crucial mechanism to create a permissive environment for infection while maintaining microglia function and inflammatory responses, sustaining neuroinflammation.

Beyond mitochondrial bioenergetics, ZIKV infection in microglia was also associated with alterations in mitochondrial dynamics, including changes in distribution and morphology. Notably, a distinct perinuclear clustering of mitochondria was observed in infected cells, a phenotype previously reported in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)-infected A594 cells [ 65 ]. This mitochondrial reorganization may be linked to the elevated microglial proliferation observed in this study, as similar clustering patterns have been described in proliferative smooth muscle cells, where dynamic mitochondrial positioning accompanies cellular morphological changes and increased motility [ 73 ]. These findings highlight the remarkable plasticity of mitochondria and reinforce the differential mitochondrial distribution observed in activated, proliferative microglia. In addition to altered distribution, ZIKV infection induced an increase in smaller-sized mitochondria, a feature with important functional implications. Smaller mitochondrial units generated through fission are thought to facilitate repair processes, helping to mitigate damage and preserve respiratory function under stress conditions [ 74 ]. This adaptation could serve as a protective mechanism, ensuring mitochondrial integrity and functionality in the face of ZIKV-induced cellular stress. Overall, these results underscore the dynamic nature of mitochondrial adaptations during ZIKV infection and suggest that mitochondrial remodeling may play a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis in response to viral challenges.

This study suggests that cytoskeletal rearrangement, metabolic shifts, and mitochondrial dynamics during ZIKV infection are influenced by both viral factors and cellular activation in response to infection. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that DHA treatment might mitigate these changes. DHA and its derivatives are well-documented for their antiviral and anti-inflammatory properties, including demonstrated activity against ZIKV in neuronal-like cells [ 26 , 43 , 75 – 77 ]. Supporting this hypothesis, our data showed that DHA treatment effectively reduced key activation-related parameters, including lipid droplet (LD) biogenesis, β-tubulin accumulation in the perinuclear region, morphological changes, and pro-inflammatory cytokine production. These results align with previous studies showing that DHA prevents neurotoxic effects in brain cells, such as inhibiting NF-κB activation under LPS stimulation [ 78 ]. Interestingly, while DHA has been reported to accumulate in LDs and their remodeling in other contexts [ 79 ], our current study showed a reduction in LD number without affecting their size. This discrepancy may stem from differences in experimental conditions, particularly the concentration of DHA used in vitro, which is known to influence its effects. Notably, the DHA concentration used in this study was lower than that typically employed in previous research [ 80 , 81 ], leading to an intriguing observation: at a lower concentration, DHA does not significantly alter homeostatic microglia but effectively prevents their activation upon ZIKV challenge. Although the general parameters remained unaffected by DHA treatment alone, a decrease in the overall number of mitochondria accompanied by an increase in smaller-sized organelles was observed. This finding suggests that DHA may impact mitochondrial dynamics in the absence of cellular stress. In 2022, a study proposed a mechanism for DHA-mediated neuroprotection through the induction of mitophagy as a protective dynamic against apoptotic cell death in neurons [ 82 ]. Notably, this report also showed an upregulation of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a key regulator of mitochondrial fission. Future studies should explore how DHA modulates mitochondrial remodeling and the impact on DHA-related anti-inflammatory effects.

Consistent with its recognized role in regulating mitochondrial function and metabolic pathways [ 83 , 84 ], DHA treatment also reduced viral load, potentially explaining its ability to suppress ZIKV-induced microglia activation. Notably, DHA downregulated the expression of AXL, a key receptor mediating ZIKV entry into host cells. This effect may be attributed to DHA’s ability to disrupt lipid raft organization within the cell membrane, thereby modulating the surface expression of membrane proteins such as AXL [ 85 ]. In addition, lipid composition is a key regulator of both transcytosis and endocytosis, raising the question of whether DHA-induced modifications to lipid rafts influence viral entry beyond its role in AXL expression modulation. While some studies suggest that polyunsaturated fatty acids can enhance membrane curvature and facilitate endocytosis [ 86 ], others indicate that lipids transported by Mfsd2a, such as DHA, create an environment that inhibits caveolae vesicle formation in endothelial cells [ 87 , 88 ]. Given that the mechanisms by which DHA reduces viral load remain incompletely understood, further investigation is needed to determine how DHA-induced lipid raft alterations impact viral entry across different cell lines, since it could be an important mechanism to be elucidated.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that systemic exposure to ZIKV in an immunocompetent animal model modulates proteins associated with mitochondrial respiration and cellular organization in the brain. In vitro analysis further revealed that ZIKV infection induces significant metabolic and morphological adaptations in human microglia cells. Unlike other brain cells, microglia maintained mitochondrial function and viability during the infection, exhibiting enhanced mitochondrial maximal respiration and metabolic reprogramming that supported both cellular activation and viral replication. DHA treatment effectively counteracted these effects, preventing microglial activation, reducing viral load, and affecting pathways critical for ZIKV entry, including the downregulation of AXL expression in the cell membrane. These findings highlight that the ability of microglia to balance metabolic demands while preserving mitochondrial function may be key for their resilience during infection, sustaining cellular functionality, while shaping the overall capacity of microglia to serve as a viral reservoir. Importantly, DHA exhibits both antiviral and anti-inflammatory properties, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic strategy to mitigate ZIKV-induced neuroinflammation and pathogenesis. The main findings were illustrated (Fig. 8 ). A key limitation is that, although microglia have been suggested to act as viral reservoirs in vitro and to present remarkable metabolic adaptations in response to ZIKV exposure, it remains unclear whether they serve this role in vivo . Further experimental models are needed to understand the clinical implications of microglia as a brain reservoir and their specific role in disease progression during ZIKV infection.

ZIKV infection reprograms microglial mitochondrial metabolism. This schematic illustrates the proposed model of ZIKV-induced metabolic reprogramming of mitochondrial metabolism in microglia during infection, based on the current experimental evidence. Infected cells demonstrated an ameboid-like phenotype, an increased number of smaller-sized mitochondria in the perinuclear region, which presented an enhanced maximal respiratory capacity. The infection led to a decrease in intracellular glucose and the accumulation of key TCA intermediates, such as citrate, succinate, fumarate, and malate (marked by red arrows). We propose that citrate is redirected to support fatty acid synthesis, as evidenced by the increase in lipid droplet biogenesis following infection, while malate contributes to redox balance. The observed decrease in glutamate may reflect its conversion to α-ketoglutarate, sustaining TCA cycle flux via anaplerotic pathways. Despite these alterations, oxidative phosphorylation remained functional, enabling microglia to meet energy needs to promote viral replication and cell survival. The anti-inflammatory omega-3 docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) treatment downregulated AXL expression, which significantly decreased viral load and the viral-related metabolic alterations, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoting a protective role against microglial activation
